opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, the goal of interpretability is to understand *why* a language model does what it does, in terms that humans can actually reason about and act on. These models are trained end to end on huge amounts of text, so nobody designed the algorithms they end up using. They just emerge. Interpretability tries to reverse-engineer those algorithms: figuring out which internal representations the model builds and how information flows through the network to produce a given output.

I think about it at a few levels. One is pure scientific curiosity. We have systems that can do remarkable things with language, and we don't really know how. That's an open question about computation and maybe even about language itself.

The second level is practical. If we can find the mechanisms behind a behavior, we can do things with that knowledge. We can predict when a model will fail, detect when it's relying on a spurious shortcut, or steer it by intervening directly on its internal representations instead of only adjusting prompts or retraining.

The third is safety and trust. As these systems get deployed in higher-stakes settings, behavioral testing alone isn't enough. You can't test every input. Understanding the internals gives you a different kind of assurance, closer to how we understand other engineered systems.

One thing I care about a lot is that interpretability should be held to rigorous standards. It's easy to tell a nice story about what a neuron or a feature "means." The real test is causal. If you intervene on that component, does the model's behavior change the way your explanation predicts? So I see the goal not just as producing explanations, but as producing explanations that are faithful to the model and actually useful, ideally evaluated against benchmarks so we can tell which methods really work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reverse-engineering internal algorithms and representations, but does not say that predicting the next token well requires building an internal model of what is happening in the text.

r002.rationale: It frames interpretability as understanding and reverse-engineering model internals, but does not identify the target as the internal model the language model builds to predict text.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, interpretability is basically the science of trying to understand what's actually going on inside these models. We have these systems that are trained on enormous amounts of data, they develop all these capabilities, and the honest truth is that nobody designed the internal mechanisms. We designed the architecture and the training objective, but the actual computation that makes the model do what it does emerged from gradient descent. So interpretability is asking: can we reverse-engineer that? Can we open up the model and say, here is the algorithm it's running, here are the concepts it represents, here is why it produced this output and not that one.

I'd say there are a couple of different goals bundled under that word, and it helps to separate them. One is the pure scientific goal. These are strange new objects, and understanding how they work is interesting in the same way that understanding the brain is interesting. A second goal is more practical: if we understand the mechanisms, we can intervene on them. We can find where a model represents some concept and edit it, steer it, or suppress a behavior we don't want. That's the direction a lot of my own work has gone, this idea of causal interventions on representations rather than just passively looking at them. And a third goal, which is the one people care most about from a safety standpoint, is being able to make guarantees. Right now when we evaluate a model, we mostly just look at its behavior on test cases. But behavior is a very thin signal. A model could behave well on everything we test and still be doing something we wouldn't endorse internally. Interpretability is the hope that we can check the mechanism directly instead of just the outputs.

I'll also say what I think the goal is not, because I think there's a common misconception. The goal isn't to produce some human-readable explanation after the fact that just sounds plausible. It's easy to generate stories about why a model did something. The bar has to be that your explanation makes predictions, that if you change the thing you claim is responsible, the behavior changes the way you said it would. That's what separates interpretability as a science from interpretability as storytelling. And honestly the field is still figuring out how to hold itself to that standard.

r002.rationale: It describes reverse-engineering a model’s algorithm and representations, but does not identify interpretability’s goal as discovering an internal model built to predict text.

astra-6.text:
I think the goal of interpretability is to understand how a model arrives at its answers, rather than just measuring whether those answers are right. We can observe the input and the output, but that leaves a lot unanswered about what happens in between.

For example, if a model answers a factual question correctly, did it retrieve a memorized association, combine several pieces of information, or exploit some shortcut in the wording? Those mechanisms can produce the same answer on one example but behave very differently in a new situation.

Ideally, we want explanations that we can test. If we think a particular component of the model is responsible for a behavior, can we change that component and predict how the behavior changes? That moves us beyond a plausible story toward a causal understanding. And that understanding could help us diagnose failures and make models more reliable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the goal of interpretability is to understand how a model arrives at its answers. We can observe what goes into a language model and what comes out, but that alone doesn’t tell us what computation happened in between.

Ideally, we’d be able to identify the internal mechanisms responsible for a behavior and test that understanding. If we think a particular component matters, can we change it and predict how the model’s behavior will change? That gives us stronger evidence than simply telling a plausible story about its activations.

The broader hope is that this understanding helps us diagnose failures, improve models, and assess when we should trust them. But explaining one behavior is still a long way from understanding an entire model.
